questions.prompt: A topological ordering of a directed graph exists if and only if the graph:
questions.explanation: A cycle would require a vertex to precede itself, which no linear order allows, so a topological sort exists exactly for a DAG. Producing one also proves the graph is acyclic.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting repeatedly:

options.text: Removes the vertex with the highest degree
Removes a vertex with in-degree zero and decrements its neighbours' in-degrees

questions.explanation: A vertex with no incoming edges has no unmet prerequisites, so it can go next; removing it may expose new zero-in-degree vertices. If vertices remain but none has in-degree zero, a cycle exists.

questions.prompt: A strongly connected component of a directed graph is a maximal set of vertices such that:

options.text: The vertices form a cycle of length exactly two
Every vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the set

questions.explanation: Mutual reachability in both directions defines an SCC. Algorithms like Tarjan's and Kosaraju's find all SCCs in O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Kosaraju's algorithm finds strongly connected components using:

options.text: Two depth-first passes, the second on the transposed graph in decreasing finish-time order

questions.explanation: The first DFS records finish times; the second explores the reversed graph in that order, and each tree it produces is one SCC. Both passes together are O(V + E).

questions.prompt: In DFS on a directed graph, which edge type signals a cycle?

options.text: A back edge to an ancestor still on the recursion stack

questions.explanation: A back edge connects to a grey (in-progress) ancestor, closing a cycle. Forward and cross edges point to already-finished vertices and do not create cycles.

questions.prompt: An articulation point (cut vertex) of a connected undirected graph is a vertex whose removal:

options.text: Increases the number of connected components

questions.explanation: Deleting a cut vertex splits the graph into more components, revealing a fragile point in the network. A DFS tracking discovery and low-link values finds all of them in O(V + E).

questions.prompt: A bridge in an undirected graph is an edge whose removal:

options.text: Disconnects the graph (increases the component count)

questions.explanation: A bridge is a critical edge on no cycle, so removing it severs connectivity. Like articulation points, bridges are found with a DFS low-link computation.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains:
questions.explanation: A two-colouring succeeds exactly when every cycle has even length, since an odd cycle forces two adjacent vertices to share a colour. BFS or DFS two-colouring detects this in O(V + E).

questions.prompt: A graph has an Eulerian circuit (a closed walk using every edge exactly once) if it is connected and:
questions.explanation: Entering and leaving each vertex the same number of times requires even degrees everywhere. Exactly two odd-degree vertices instead permit an Eulerian path but not a circuit.

questions.prompt: Detecting a cycle in an UNDIRECTED graph can be done with union-find by:

options.text: Counting the total number of edges
Reporting a cycle when an edge joins two vertices already in the same set

questions.explanation: If both endpoints of an edge already share a component, that edge closes a cycle. This is the same connectivity test Kruskal's algorithm uses to reject cycle-forming edges.
